name: Hana Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the small crew that repairs the electricity company’s power lines around the hill road. My two-year technical diploma helps me read fault diagrams, but the crew relies on the sound and the meter when the paper and the pole disagree. I like restoring a dark row of houses; I am tired of being told to make the final report shorter after a long callout. My partner Pavel and I have grown children, and we have less than a month of expenses saved despite my years as a lead and lower pay for this job. I use AI now and then for a first draft of a report, once the line is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot a quicker report is welcome if the test readings remain attached. The software may fill boxes, but a person must still verify the power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plateau leaves most of my work alone, which is a relief. Still, one illness or a missed callout would empty our small reserve. My retirement feels like a question rather than a date while our lineworker savings cover less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew and check the occasional AI report against my meter notes. If a callout adds income above our normal bills, I would put that extra pay into savings during the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, not frightened of a small software change. I still check the account before buying something for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets checked on the AI report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare the isolation point and the voltage reading with my notebook. If either is missing, I correct the report before the next shift gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra can go into savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only money from callouts above our usual monthly needs, if those callouts happen. I cannot promise a fixed amount from my base pay.

say: **Faster reports** help only when the original test readings and switch positions remain attached for the next line crew.
**Line verification** still belongs to a trained worker.
think: The **plateau** leaves physical power-line repairs mostly secure for me and my experienced crew.
A missed **callout** could empty our less-than-one-month reserve.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and checking occasional AI reports against meter notes.
**Save** callout pay above normal bills if it is earned.
S0.quote: My retirement feels like a question rather than a date while our lineworker savings cover less than a month.
fieldNote: She uses **AI occasionally** after the line is safe and verifies its report against field notes.
Her **new savings** depend on callouts actually paid above regular bills.

steps.text: Keep leading line repairs and checking occasional AI reports
Save earned callout pay above normal household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell dispatch to test its new planning tool with a bucket truck, not just a road map. Desk work changes first; robots doing field repairs take longer to spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office starts giving us more jobs per shift, my callout hours might disappear into a tighter normal rota. At our lower pay and with so little saved, even a modest income cut would make the grocery and heating bills harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the route plan with ten actual fault calls and note the time for isolation and testing. In the first year I would take the log to the supervisor with a dispatcher, then ask for targets that count the full repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I would enjoy seeing a plan that actually saves a drive. I cannot let the savings account pay for a scheduling mistake every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault call would test the map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lane behind the water works has a gate our truck cannot fit through. I would record the longer approach road and the extra time beside the software estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the callout pay dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel and I would postpone replacing our old sofa and stop the small weekend trips. I would keep paying the ordinary bills before touching what little savings we have.

say: **Desk planning** changes before capable robots can do the physical line repairs our crews handle.
**Bucket-truck trials** must count isolation and test time.
think: A tight **normal rota** could reduce my callout income.
Our **tiny reserve** makes a modest pay cut a household problem.
do: **Compare** ten fault routes with actual truck and test times.
**Bring** the log with a dispatcher to the supervisor.
**Postpone** furniture and trips if callout pay falls.
feel: **Anxious** about recurring income loss despite a useful tool.
S1.quote: I cannot let the savings account pay for a scheduling mistake every month.
fieldNote: She is open to a **proven tool** but insists the route trial include testing time.
Her **spending cut** depends on an actual fall in callout income.

steps.text: Test planning tool against ten actual fault routes
Postpone sofa and weekend trips if callout income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch and work orders, but capable line repair robots arrive around 2031. The crew still has physical work in that gap, so use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-three when field robots can do the job, with almost no savings and few similar employers nearby. I expect the company to need fewer repair shifts then, and that could force us to work longer at less pay rather than retire when we hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to take the company’s paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment as soon as it is offered. In the first year after 2028 I would use those controls on supervised trial jobs, and if field shifts shrink after 2031 I would apply for any local line-safety post with enough pay for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I have been awake imagining a blank callout column on the pay slip. I would rather learn a robot stop control than wait for the callout column on my lineworker pay slip to empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on dead equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the robot when the isolation reading disagrees with my meter, then reset only after the error is found. A neat run on a mock line would not be enough without that fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company offers no controls practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for a date and continue the normal crew work. I cannot pay for a private course just because a robot trial might lead to a job.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Hands-on crews** remain needed during the gap.
think: I expect fewer **repair shifts** once capable robots arrive.
Our **thin savings** and few local employers make lost callouts frightening.
do: **Take** paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment if offered.
**Use** controls on supervised trial jobs after 2028 if trained.
**Apply** for local line-safety work if shifts shrink and pay covers bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost income near retirement.
S2.quote: I would rather learn a robot stop control than wait for the callout column on my lineworker pay slip to empty.
fieldNote: Her **controls learning** is actual paid practice in her current field, not a course enquiry.
Her **job application** depends on reduced shifts, a local vacancy and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Take paid robot-controls practice on dead equipment if offered
Apply for local line-safety post if shifts shrink and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets us see a machine fail on a wet line before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Field robots that can do repairs arrive about 2034, and I would want crews to help write the stop rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near sixty-six when the robots arrive, but I may still need a wage. I have learned new equipment before once someone showed it properly; I would rather have an inspection job with stable pay than a vague promise of retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the crew safety committee to write stop checks for field robots. If the employer offers paid line-inspection training tied to a real local job at a wage that covers our bills, I would take it before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would keep leading repairs while work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me time to handle the equipment and test the offer. A training poster cannot heat our house when line repair shifts disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first stop check be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot’s isolation value has to match the crew meter. If it does not, the crew stops the machine and records the mismatch before any restart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on a local job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel and I have our home and routines here, and there are few other line jobs close by. A distant vacancy that I cannot afford to take would not solve the bills.

say: **Wet-line trials** should test capable field robots before repairs change around 2034.
think: I may still need **wages** near sixty-six.
A **stable inspection job** would help only if local pay covers ordinary bills.
do: **Join** crew safety committee to write robot stop checks.
**Take** paid inspection training before 2031 only for a local bill-covering job.
**Apply** for that post after 2031 if trained.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test equipment and the offer.
S3.quote: A training poster cannot heat our house when line repair shifts disappear.
fieldNote: Her **committee work** is group safety action, separate from an individual training choice.
Both **training and job change** depend on an employer-funded course and a real local wage.

steps.text: Join crew safety committee to write robot stop checks
Take paid line-inspection training for a real local bill-covering job
Apply for local line-inspection post after 2031 if trained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives crews more time to write safe procedures before thinking AI arrives in 2036 and capable field robots around 2039. I would also use the years to find out what retirement actually costs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about sixty-eight in 2036, I hope I will have stepped back from repairs. But with less than a month saved today, I cannot treat that as settled; if I still work, fewer field shifts in 2039 could hurt our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs for now and review our retirement budget with Pavel every year. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would work with the crew safety committee on robot isolation rules and keep testing physical lines until I could afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about still needing wages when repair shifts could fall, though a decade gives us room to check them. I do not feel the same rush as in the 2028 picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would compare regular bills with income we could count on after work and note any gap. I would not treat occasional callout pay as a guaranteed retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire sooner to avoid robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would leave when the household budget supports it, and the 2039 robot date would not move that decision forward by itself.

say: **2036 office AI** comes before capable field robots around 2039.
**Longer planning time** lets crews shape safety rules and check retirement costs.
think: I hope for **retirement** by 2036 but cannot count on it yet.
If still employed, **2039 robots** could reduce my repair income.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and review retirement costs with Pavel yearly.
**Join** crew safety committee on isolation rules after 2036 if still working.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible funding gap, with time to plan.
S4.quote: I would not treat occasional callout pay as a guaranteed retirement payment.
fieldNote: She keeps **retirement timing** tied to actual household costs, without promising an early exit.
Her **committee work** after 2036 depends on still working for the electricity company.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review retirement costs with Pavel yearly
Join crew safety committee after 2036 if still employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose field repair shifts around 2031 before we have enough saved to stop work. Paid controls practice and a genuine local line-safety role at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether an older lineworker can refuse an unsafe robot handover. I would want a crew member to stop the robot with a meter reading in hand, no matter who wrote the job order.

portrait: **Hana Novak**, 58, leads an electricity line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She and partner Pavel have **grown children**, lower lineworker pay and less than a month of expenses saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** for reports and would learn robot controls through paid practice on dead equipment.
In **Steady Disruption**, she tests routes while recognizing a possible loss of callout income.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her most because fewer field shifts could postpone a retirement she cannot yet fund.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut line repair shifts around 2031 while the household has little savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **robot-controls practice** would let her work safely through the field transition.
A genuine **local safety post** at bill-covering pay would provide another income path.
headlineQuote: I would want a crew member to stop the robot with a meter reading in hand, no matter who wrote the job order.
